analysis.one_liner: Provides loan guarantees, tax credits, and Defense Department contracts for coal-to-liquid fuel plants.
analysis.headline: The Coal-to-Liquid Fuel Promotion Act of 2006, introduced by Sen. Bunning with 10 cosponsors from both parties, never left the Senate Finance Committee and received no vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have used federal money to jump-start an industry that turns coal into liquid fuel: it adds large coal-to-liquid plants to the Department of Energy's loan guarantee program, creates a 20% investment tax credit for such projects, lets companies write off plant equipment immediately, and extends an existing alternative fuel tax credit for coal-derived fuel through 2020. It also authorizes the Defense Department to contract with private companies to build and run coal-to-liquid facilities on or near military installations, and funds Air Force testing of synthetic jet fuel.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that would build coal-to-liquid plants and the coal industry that supplies them. The bill gives them federal loan guarantees (up to ten projects capped at 100,000 barrels per day of capacity), a 20% investment tax credit on up to $2 billion of qualified investment, immediate expensing of plant equipment, a planning loan program backed by $200 million in appropriations, and a guaranteed market channel through Defense Department contracts and Air Force jet-fuel procurement.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal companies and synthetic fuel developers

how_it_helps.text: Adds large-scale coal-to-liquid facilities producing at least 10,000 barrels per day to the projects eligible for Department of Energy loan guarantees, with up to ten guarantees and a 100,000 barrel-per-day capacity cap [S2][S3].
Creates a 20% investment tax credit for qualifying coal-to-liquid projects, available to 10 project sponsors covering up to $2 billion of qualified investment [S3].

Lets companies deduct the full cost of coal-to-liquid process equipment in the year it is placed in service, and extends the alternative fuel credit for Fischer-Tropsch coal fuel through September 30, 2020 [S3].
Authorizes $200 million for a federal planning loan program and directs the Energy Secretary to write rules supporting coal-to-liquid facilities on federal land and military bases [S2][S3].

Amends military fuel procurement law so the Defense Secretary can contract with private companies to develop and operate coal-to-liquid facilities on or near military installations, with agreements running up to 25 years, and allocates $10 million for the Air Force Research Laboratory to test and qualify coal-derived jet fuel [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, in three ways: they back the loan guarantees if projects default, they lose federal revenue from the new tax credit, expensing, and the extended alternative fuel credit, and they fund the $200 million planning loan program and $10 million for Air Force testing. The public also bears the environmental cost of expanding coal-based fuel production, since the bill subsidizes carbon-capture property but does not require it.

drawbacks.text: The bill shifts large financial risk to taxpayers: loan guarantees mean that if the plants fail commercially, the federal government — and taxpayers — absorb the losses [S3].

The tax provisions drain federal revenue: a 20% investment credit on up to $2 billion of investment, immediate expensing of equipment, and an extended alternative fuel credit running through 2020 all reduce money available for other purposes [S3].

Producing liquid fuel from coal through the Fischer-Tropsch process is far more carbon-intensive than refining conventional fuel unless the carbon emissions are captured and sequestered; the bill allows credit for carbon-capture property but does not require it, so subsidized plants could lock in a high-carbon fuel source for decades [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would open a domestic fuel source derived from U.S. coal and give the military a homegrown jet fuel supply, which its bipartisan sponsors framed as energy security. But the costs are substantial and one-sided: taxpayers would underwrite the loans, absorb the revenue loss from layered tax breaks, and carry the environmental burden of a coal-based fuel industry whose carbon capture was optional rather than required. The private developers would keep the profits; the downside risks — guarantee defaults and emissions — would land on the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Jim Bunning introduced the bill on May 26, 2006, joined by original cosponsors Sens. Obama, Lugar, Burns, and Pryor [S3].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No further action was taken — no committee markup, no floor vote — before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].
The bill attracted 10 cosponsors: 8 Republicans and 2 Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, taxpayers avoided the loan guarantee exposure, the tax revenue loss, and the emissions of a subsidized coal-fuel industry; coal-to-liquid developers gained nothing. Had it passed, the coal and synthetic fuel industries would have been the main beneficiaries.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers, who avoided the subsidies and risks

for.name: Sen. Jim Bunning
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it [S3][S5].

for.name: Sens. Richard Lugar, Conrad Burns, and Mark Pryor
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced [S3].

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Chuck Grassley)
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled action on the bill
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred — no markup, no vote — leaving it to expire at the end of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan: of the bill's 10 cosponsors, 8 were Republicans and 2 were Democrats, and original cosponsors included two Democrats (Obama and Pryor) alongside three Republicans [S3][S4]; no votes were ever taken.

industries.note: The bill creates federal demand and financial backing for converting coal into transportation fuel through loan guarantees, tax credits, military procurement, and Strategic Petroleum Reserve storage of up to 20% coal-derived products. The profits would flow to coal producers while the guarantee risk, revenue cost, and carbon emissions fall on the public [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Synthetic fuel and Fischer-Tropsch plant developers
industries.note: Developers of large coal-to-liquid plants would receive a 20% investment tax credit on up to $2 billion of investment, immediate equipment expensing, federal loan guarantees, $200 million in planning loans, and Defense Department contracts running up to 25 years — a heavily subsidized channel for a fuel whose carbon capture was optional [S3].

industries.industry: Military aviation and jet fuel supply
industries.note: The bill funds $10 million for Air Force testing and qualification of coal-derived jet fuel and eases procurement of synthetic fuel, offering the military a domestic alternative to imported oil [S2][S3].
